summary: This document extends the way Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) carries multicast traffic, which earlier RFCs 4761 and 4762 handled with unicast tunnels. Those tunnels can waste bandwidth when a lot of multicast data is sent. It describes solutions to overcome a subset of those limits.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine mailing the same newsletter to a whole class by sending one separate copy down every road. This document finds smarter ways to share one copy so the roads are not clogged.

questions: how does multicast work in vpls
what is ingress replication in vpls
what is an inclusive tree in vpls
what is a selective tree in vpls
what is the pmsi tunnel attribute
subtitle: How VPLS carries multicast and broadcast over shared trees in the provider network instead of copying every packet to every edge router.

tldr.problem: VPLS multicast as defined in RFC 4761 and RFC 4762 uses ingress replication: the ingress router copies each multicast or broadcast packet to every other edge router over unicast tunnels, which wastes bandwidth when traffic is heavy.
tldr.mechanism: The ingress provider edge router sends the packets down a point-to-multipoint tree in the provider network (an RSVP-TE or mLDP P2MP LSP). One tree can serve one or several VPLS instances, and BGP announces which tree carries what.
tldr.outcome: Heavy multicast uses far less core bandwidth, at the cost of tree state in the provider network. High-bandwidth streams can be moved to Selective trees that reach only interested routers.

today: RFC 7117 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the specification for multicast trees in VPLS built on RFC 4761 and RFC 4762.

sections.title: The Problem with Ingress Replication
sections.content:
RFC 4761 and RFC 4762 carry VPLS multicast and broadcast over pseudowires on unicast point-to-point RSVP-TE or multipoint-to-point LDP LSPs. This document calls that approach ingress replication: the ingress Provider Edge (PE) router copies a packet from a customer edge (CE) router once for each egress PE and sends each copy through a unicast tunnel.

That can use bandwidth badly in the MPLS network when a lot of multicast or broadcast traffic is sent. It may be acceptable when traffic is low or few replications happen per outgoing interface. Otherwise the RFC wants multicast trees in the service provider (SP) network, built as P2MP LSPs signaled with P2MP RSVP-TE or Multipoint LDP (mLDP). The procedures apply to both RFC 4761 and RFC 4762.
sections.plainLanguage: Making a separate copy for every receiver is fine for a few people but clogs the road for a big crowd. A tree of shared roads sends one copy until the road splits.

sections.title: Inclusive and Selective Trees
sections.content:
The document uses prefix C for customer packets and P for provider packets. It defines two kinds of tree, plus aggregate versions of each:

  • Inclusive tree: one tree carrying all multicast traffic of one VPLS instance on a given PE. It reaches every PE in that instance, so a PE may receive streams it has no receivers for. It can carry IP and non-IP multicast.
  • Aggregate Inclusive tree: one tree shared by more than one VPLS instance on a PE.
  • Selective tree: a tree for a specified set of IP multicast streams of one VPLS instance, reaching only a subset of PEs, those on the path to receivers. It is meant for specific streams such as high-bandwidth ones, and only for IP multicast.
  • Aggregate Selective tree: a Selective tree whose streams come from more than one VPLS instance.

An SP can use either or both kinds for a given VPLS on a PE, based on local configuration. Unknown-unicast flooding may still use ingress replication or may use the new trees. The benefit of trees comes at the cost of state in the SP network and the overhead to maintain it.
sections.plainLanguage: An Inclusive tree is a bus that stops at every house on the route. A Selective tree is a special bus that only visits the houses where someone wants that particular show.

sections.title: Building and Advertising Trees
sections.content:
PEs find each other with the BGP VPLS auto-discovery of RFC 4761 and RFC 6074. A PE with a VSI originates an Intra-AS A-D route in MP-IBGP. If it uses an Inclusive tree, it MUST put the type and identity of the tree in the PMSI Tunnel attribute (reused from RFC 6514). Receiving PEs that match on Route Targets then join or expect the tree. The supported tunnel types are RSVP-TE P2MP LSP and mLDP P2MP LSP, and an implementation MUST support both.

For RSVP-TE, the root learns the leaves from the A-D routes and signals the LSP per RFC 4875. The egress PE assigns a non-special-purpose MPLS label for the LSP and discards traffic received before the binding is known. For mLDP, each egress PE SHOULD join by sending LDP label mapping messages for the P2MP FEC learned over BGP, per RFC 6388.

The decision to bind VPLS instances or streams to a tree is a local matter on the ingress PE. Aggregate trees MUST use MPLS encapsulation (RFC 5332).
sections.plainLanguage: Each router shouts over a shared bulletin board which bus line carries which show. The others read the board and hop onto the right bus.

sections.title: Aggregation and Demultiplexing
sections.content:
Aggregation means carrying several VPLS instances on one tree. It bounds the multicast state P-routers must keep: the number of trees a PE roots is proportional to its VPLS instances divided by the Aggregation Factor. Because the tree is shared, the egress PE needs to know which VPLS a packet belongs to. The root therefore assigns an inner upstream-assigned label (RFC 5331) per VPLS, and the outer tree label supplies the label space in which to look it up. The inner label is only unique within the context of its root.

For this to work, Penultimate Hop Popping MUST be disabled, and an egress PE MUST NOT advertise implicit or explicit null for a tree bound to VPLS instances. With one tree for one VPLS, the tree label alone identifies the VPLS. Aggregation needs two MPLS labels, the same as ingress replication does, so MTU is not affected.

The trade-off is congruency. If the VPLS instances on a tree have different members, a PE may get traffic for VPLS instances it does not belong to. The RFC does not mandate rules for choosing what to aggregate; that is left to heuristics, configuration or offline tools, and implementations should offer controls.
sections.plainLanguage: When one bus carries kids from several schools, each kid wears a school badge. The badge tells the stop which school's classroom to go to.

sections.title: Switching to Selective Trees
sections.content:
A stream with lots of traffic can be moved from an Inclusive tree to a Selective tree whose leaves are only PEs with receivers. A trigger can be as simple as bandwidth, or a "pseudo-wasted bandwidth" test: bandwidth multiplied by the number of uninterested PEs above a threshold.

The source PE announces the binding with an S-PMSI A-D route in the MCAST-VPLS address family. Source and group may be specific addresses or wildcards. If the PE sets the Leaf Information Required flag in the PMSI Tunnel attribute, egress PEs with matching snooped IGMP or MLD state answer with leaf A-D routes, which gives the root explicit tracking of receivers. Procedures for PIM with join suppression enabled are out of scope.

To avoid loss without duplication, the source PE MUST wait a "switchover" delay (configurable, RECOMMENDED) after announcing and before sending the stream on the Selective tree. No packet is ever sent on both trees. For RSVP-TE, an egress PE MUST switch only after the announcement arrives and the LSP is set up to it.
sections.plainLanguage: When one show is popular with only a few houses, give it its own small bus. Wait a moment before moving it over so nobody misses the start or sees it twice.

sections.title: Inter-AS Options
sections.content:
Four models of inter-AS VPLS are covered. An implementation MUST support options (a), (b) and (c), and MAY support (e).

  • Option (a): ASBRs act as PEs and view each other as CEs over VLAN sub-interfaces, with a MAC lookup at the ASBR. Trees stay inside each AS and no VPLS A-D routes are exchanged.
  • Option (e): like (a), but ASBRs connect VSIs over an MPLS pseudowire.
  • Option (b): segmented inter-AS trees. Each AS builds its own segment, possibly with a different technology, and ASBRs stitch segments together without needing a VSI or MAC lookup. ASBRs re-advertise A-D routes and answer with leaf A-D routes; only one ASBR per AS accepts traffic for a given tree.
  • Option (c): a single non-segmented tree spans the ASes, so every AS on the path must support the tunnel technology. ASBRs only do MPLS forwarding. For mLDP without RFC 6512, PE loopback addresses must be reachable in the IGP of the other AS.

Selective trees follow the same options. Segmented Selective trees MUST be implemented for option (b) and MAY be used for (c). An ASBR MAY merge an upstream Selective tree into a downstream Inclusive tree if both routes come from the same AS and carry exactly the same Route Targets, which applies to option (b) only.
sections.plainLanguage: When a message must cross several cities, each city can run its own local delivery system, and the border posts hand parcels from one to the next. Or one long route can run straight through all of them.

sections.title: BGP Extensions and Packet Forwarding
sections.content:
The PMSI_TUNNEL attribute (reused from RFC 6514) may carry tunnel types 0 (none), 1 (RSVP-TE P2MP LSP), 2 (LDP P2MP LSP) and 6 (Ingress Replication). The new MCAST-VPLS NLRI has a one-octet Route Type, a one-octet Length, and a type-specific part. Type 3 is the Selective Tree A-D route (RD, source, group, originating router address) and type 4 is the Leaf A-D route (a route key plus originating router address). It is carried with AFI 25 and the new SAFI.

On the data path, the ingress PE pushes a VPLS label and the tree label for an Aggregate tree, or only the tree label for a single-VPLS tree. IP multicast with a Selective tree uses it; non-IP multicast and broadcast use the Inclusive tree. The egress PE looks up the outer label to pick the label space, then the inner label to find the VSI.

For packets arriving at the ingress PE, a Selective tree for the stream MUST be used if one exists; otherwise a (C-*, C-*) Selective tree, then an Inclusive tree, SHOULD be used. Unknown unicast may also use trees, but then egress PEs MUST be able to learn MAC addresses from tree traffic by identifying the sender PE. Switching to a pseudowire after learning can cause reordering.
sections.plainLanguage: Each parcel gets two stickers: one says which bus it rides, and one says which classroom it is for. The last stop reads both to deliver it correctly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 4761 and RFC 4762 apply. A compromised control plane could send one VPLS's multicast data to another VPLS, black-hole it, send it to an eavesdropper, or exploit replication within a tree to amplify a denial-of-service attack.

Because BGP is the control plane, techniques such as RFC 5925 help authenticate messages, which makes spoofed updates and withdrawals harder. In multi-AS methods (b) and (c) this includes protecting the inter-AS BGP sessions. Such techniques do not keep MPLS labels private, so someone who knows the labels and can reach the data path could eavesdrop; that path is assumed to run over trusted nodes and links. MPLS labels must be accepted only from valid interfaces, and this matters most for multi-AS VPLS.
sections.plainLanguage: The notice board must not be forged, or parcels go to the wrong room. The roads inside the delivery company are assumed trustworthy, and parcels are only accepted from proper doors.
